:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,3).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}))) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(x{y}^{2})}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the constant multiple rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,3)} & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{1+{1}^{2}\cdot {3}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{9}{1+81} \\  & =\frac{9}{82}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-8{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(1) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the constant multiple rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{4})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{2}) & =2\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4})+8{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})-8\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{3}+8{y}^{2}\cdot 2x-8\cdot 2x \\  & =8{x}^{3}+16x{y}^{2}-16x\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x}-y{z}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{z}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})-{z}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =x{y}^{x-1}-{z}^{3}\cdot (1) \\  & =x{y}^{x-1}-{z}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{3y-2x}{7y-6x}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{(7y-6x)^{2}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{3y-2x}{7y-6x}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(3y-2x)\cdot (7y-6x)-(3y-2x)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(7y-6x)}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (7y-6x)-(3y-2x)\cdot (-6)}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-14y+12x+18y-12x}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4y}{(7y-6x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=4y.

:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y))\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot 1}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)){e}^{x+y}}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y).
$$

:question/problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=xy\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))) \\  & =x((1)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡({y}^{2})\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy{sec}^{2}⁡({y}^{2})\cdot (2y) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x+y}+{x}^{2}\sqrt{y},$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(3,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y}+{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y))+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (0+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(3,1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3+1}}+\frac{{3}^{2}}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{19}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ for $f(x,y,z)={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}) \\  & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(4y-x{z}^{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(4y-x{z}^{4}) & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂z}(4y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{4})) \\  & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot (0-x\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{4})) \\  & =-{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot x\cdot 4{z}^{3} \\  & =-4x{z}^{3}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-4x{z}^{3}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}.
$$

:question/problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) & =(3{x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{x}^{3}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{3}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot (1) \\  & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{3}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3}).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differenciation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (2x+{y}^{2}\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,\sqrt{3}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find $g_y(x,y,z)$ for $g(x,y,z)=(x+z)\sin y+(y+z)\cos x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, holding $x$ and $z$ fixed. Thus $x+z$ and $\cos x$ are constants, while $y+z$ has derivative $1$.

Using the sum and constant multiple rules,

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_y(x,y,z)&=(x+z)\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\sin y)+\cos x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y+z)\\
&=(x+z)\cos y+\cos x(1+0)\\
&=(x+z)\cos y+\cos x.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $h(x,y,z)=z\sqrt{4x^2+y^2},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}$ at the point $(-2,3,-1).$
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $x$, holding $y$ and $z$ fixed. The factor $z$ stays constant, and the square root requires the chain rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}&=z\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4x^2+y^2}}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(4x^2+y^2)\\
&=\frac{z}{2\sqrt{4x^2+y^2}}(8x+0)\\
&=\frac{4xz}{\sqrt{4x^2+y^2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $x=-2$, $y=3$, and $z=-1$. The radicand is $25>0$, so this derivative is defined at the point.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\right|_{(-2,3,-1)}&=\frac{4(-2)(-1)}{\sqrt{4(-2)^2+3^2}}\\
&=\frac{8}{\sqrt{25}}\\
&=\frac{8}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ for $f(x,y,z)=xy^2+z^3.$ Treat $x$ and $z$ as constants.
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ and $z$ fixed. The factor $x$ is a constant multiplier, and $z^3$ is independent of $y$.

Using the sum, constant multiple, and power rules,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^2)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(z^3)\\
&=x(2y)+0\\
&=2xy.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ for $f(x,y)=x^2y\sin x+y^3.$
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant. The term $y^3$ therefore has derivative zero, and $y$ is a constant multiplier in the first term:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=y\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2\sin x)+0.
$$

Apply the product rule to $x^2\sin x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y\left(\frac{\partial x^2}{\partial x}\sin x+x^2\frac{\partial\sin x}{\partial x}\right)\\
&=y(2x\sin x+x^2\cos x).
\end{aligned}
$$

Both product-rule terms are needed; differentiating both factors and multiplying their derivatives would omit them.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=(x+y^2)(e^{xy}+\ln y)$, evaluate $f_y(2,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $x$ as constant. Both grouped factors depend on $y$, so neither entire factor is a constant multiplier. Let

$$
u=x+y^2,\qquad v=e^{xy}+\ln y.
$$

Their partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_y&=2y,\\
v_y&=e^{xy}\frac{\partial(xy)}{\partial y}+\frac{1}{y}\\
&=xe^{xy}+\frac{1}{y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The product rule gives

$$
f_y(x,y)=2y(e^{xy}+\ln y)+(x+y^2)\left(xe^{xy}+\frac{1}{y}\right).
$$

At $(2,1)$, we have $\ln1=0$ and $e^{xy}=e^2$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(2,1)&=2(e^2+0)+(2+1)(2e^2+1)\\
&=2e^2+6e^2+3\\
&=8e^2+3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Although $\ln1=0$, its derivative contributes $1/y=1$ at this point. That contribution must be included before evaluating.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=ye^{xy}-x^2y^2$, evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(2,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, keeping $x$ constant. Use the product rule on $ye^{xy}$ and the constant multiple rule on $x^2y^2$:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=1\cdot e^{xy}+y\frac{\partial e^{xy}}{\partial y}-2x^2y.
$$

The exponential also requires the chain rule. Since $\dfrac{\partial(xy)}{\partial y}=x$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=e^{xy}+y e^{xy}x-2x^2y\\
&=(1+xy)e^{xy}-2x^2y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $x=2$ and $y=1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(2,1)&=(1+2\cdot1)e^{2\cdot1}-2\cdot2^2\cdot1\\
&=3e^2-8.
\end{aligned}
$$

Keep the $y$ dependence until after differentiating. Substituting both coordinates first would leave only a number.

:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\ln(1+e^{xy})+x^2y,
$$

evaluate both partial derivatives at $(1,2)$.

$f_x(1,2)=$

{{field-1}}

$f_y(1,2)=$

{{field-2}}
:question/worked-solution:
For $f_x$, treat $y$ as a constant. The logarithmic term requires the chain rule twice: first through the logarithm, then through the exponential. The term $x^2y$ uses the constant multiple rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=\frac{1}{1+e^{xy}}\cdot e^{xy}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xy)+2xy\\
&=\frac{ye^{xy}}{1+e^{xy}}+2xy.
\end{aligned}
$$

For $f_y$, instead treat $x$ as a constant. In particular, the inner derivative of $xy$ is now $x$, and the derivative of $x^2y$ is $x^2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)&=\frac{1}{1+e^{xy}}\cdot e^{xy}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy)+x^2\\
&=\frac{xe^{xy}}{1+e^{xy}}+x^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate each derivative at $x=1$, $y=2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(1,2)&=\frac{2e^2}{1+e^2}+2\cdot1\cdot2=\frac{2e^2}{1+e^2}+4,\\
f_y(1,2)&=\frac{e^2}{1+e^2}+1^2=\frac{e^2}{1+e^2}+1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two values differ because a different variable is held constant in each derivative. Also, $1+e^{xy}>0$ for all real $x,y$, so the logarithm and both derivatives are defined at the given point.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=e^{xy}+x^2y$, evaluate $f_y(2,0).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant. Use the sum rule, then the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(e^{xy})+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2y)\\
&=e^{xy}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy)+x^2\cdot\frac{\partial y}{\partial y}\\
&=xe^{xy}+x^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $x=2$ and $y=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(2,0)&=2e^{2\cdot0}+2^2\\
&=2\cdot1+4\\
&=6.
\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative is taken before evaluating; substituting both coordinates into $f$ first would leave only a number.

:question/problem: Find $f_y(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\ln(x+y^2).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant. Let $u=x+y^2$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\ln u=\frac{1}{u},\qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0+2y.
$$

Applying the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)&=\frac{1}{x+y^2}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x+y^2)\\
&=\frac{1}{x+y^2}\cdot 2y\\
&=\frac{2y}{x+y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The formula applies where $x+y^2>0$, the domain of the logarithm.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x^2-y^2}{e^{y-x}}$, evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(1,0)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant. In particular, the chain rule gives

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}e^{y-x}=-e^{y-x}.
$$

Apply the quotient rule before evaluating at the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}
&=\frac{2x e^{y-x}-(x^2-y^2)(-e^{y-x})}{(e^{y-x})^2} \\
&=\frac{2x+x^2-y^2}{e^{y-x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $x=1$ and $y=0$:

$$
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(1,0)}
=\frac{2+1-0}{e^{-1}}=3e.
$$

The denominator is always positive, so the function and this derivative are defined at the given point.

:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{e^{xy^2}}{x+y^2},
$$

find $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$, where $x+y^2\ne0$.

Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2x+3y}{x-2y}$. The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{h(x,y)}{(x-2y)^2}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant. The numerator and denominator derivatives are

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2x+3y)=3,
\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x-2y)=-2.
$$

Using the quotient rule,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}
&=\frac{3(x-2y)-(2x+3y)(-2)}{(x-2y)^2} \\
&=\frac{3x-6y+4x+6y}{(x-2y)^2} \\
&=\frac{7x}{(x-2y)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing with the supplied form gives $h(x,y)=7x$. These formulas apply where $x-2y\ne0$.

For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{- 2 x^{2} - 3 y^{2} - 2}{\sqrt{y}},
$$

evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(-1,1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=- 2 x^{2} - 3 y^{2} - 2$ and $D=\sqrt{y}$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=- 6 y, \\
D_{y}&=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{y}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the square root use $D_{y}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$.  Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- 6 y\right)D-N\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{y}}\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{2 x^{2} - 9 y^{2} + 2}{2\left(y\right)\sqrt{y}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step multiplies the numerator and denominator by $2\sqrt{y}$ and collects the numerator terms. Now substitute the point, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(-1,1)}&=\frac{\left(-6\right)\left(1\right)-\left(-7\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(1\right)^2} \\
&=- \frac{5}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 These expressions apply where $y>0$.

:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{3 x^{2} + y^{2} - 1}{e^{x - y}},
$$

evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(-1,2)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=3 x^{2} + y^{2} - 1$ and $D=e^{x - y}$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=2 y, \\
D_{y}&=- e^{x - y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule differentiates the exponent first; its inner derivative is $-1$. Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(2 y\right)D-N\left(- e^{x - y}\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{3 x^{2} + y^{2} + 2 y - 1}{e^{x - y}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step factors the common nonzero exponential $e^{x - y}$ from the numerator. Cancel that factor with one copy in the squared denominator. Now substitute the point, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(-1,2)}&=\frac{\left(4\right)\left(\frac{1}{e^{3}}\right)-\left(6\right)\left(- \frac{1}{e^{3}}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{e^{3}}\right)^2} \\
&=10 e^{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 These expressions apply where $e^{x - y}\ne0$.

:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{- 2 x y - 3}{2 x - 2 y - 1},
$$

evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(0,-1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $y$ constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Write $N=- 2 x y - 3$ and $D=2 x - 2 y - 1$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{x}&=- 2 y, \\
D_{x}&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

 Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\frac{N_{x}D-ND_{x}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- 2 y\right)D-N\left(2\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{4 y^{2} + 2 y + 6}{\left(2 x - 2 y - 1\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step distributes the subtraction and collects like terms. Now substitute the point, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(0,-1)}&=\frac{\left(2\right)\left(1\right)-\left(-3\right)\left(2\right)}{\left(1\right)^2} \\
&=8.
\end{aligned}
$$

 These expressions apply where $2 x - 2 y - 1\ne0$.

:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{- 3 x^{2} - 2 y^{2}}{e^{- x + y}},
$$

evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(-1,1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $y$ constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Write $N=- 3 x^{2} - 2 y^{2}$ and $D=e^{- x + y}$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{x}&=- 6 x, \\
D_{x}&=- e^{- x + y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule differentiates the exponent first; its inner derivative is $-1$. Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\frac{N_{x}D-ND_{x}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- 6 x\right)D-N\left(- e^{- x + y}\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{- 3 x^{2} - 6 x - 2 y^{2}}{e^{- x + y}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step factors the common nonzero exponential $e^{- x + y}$ from the numerator. Cancel that factor with one copy in the squared denominator. Now substitute the point, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(-1,1)}&=\frac{\left(6\right)\left(e^{2}\right)-\left(-5\right)\left(- e^{2}\right)}{\left(e^{2}\right)^2} \\
&=\frac{1}{e^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 These expressions apply where $e^{- x + y}\ne0$.

:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{x y - 3}{- x + 2 y},
$$

evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(-1,1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=x y - 3$ and $D=- x + 2 y$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=x, \\
D_{y}&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

 Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(x\right)D-N\left(2\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{6 - x^{2}}{\left(- x + 2 y\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step distributes the subtraction and collects like terms. Now substitute the point, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(-1,1)}&=\frac{\left(-1\right)\left(3\right)-\left(-4\right)\left(2\right)}{\left(3\right)^2} \\
&=\frac{5}{9}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 These expressions apply where $- x + 2 y\ne0$.

:question/problem: For $f(x,y)=y \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$, evaluate $f_y(2,\sqrt{5})$. Assume $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$.
For $f(x,y)=x \tan{\left(x y^{2} \right)}$, evaluate $f_x(\frac{\pi}{16},-2)$. Assume $\cos(x y^{2})\ne0$.
For $f(x,y)=y^{2} \tan{\left(x^{2} y \right)}$, evaluate $f_y(-1,- \frac{\pi}{4})$. Assume $\cos(x^{2} y)\ne0$.
For $f(x,y)=x^{2} e^{x} \cos{\left(y \right)}$, evaluate $f_x(2,0)$.
For $f(x,y)=x y \cos{\left(x \right)} - \sin{\left(x \right)}$, evaluate $f_x(- \pi,2)$.
For the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2 x^{2} + y^{2}}$, evaluate $f_x(1,- \sqrt{2})$.
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=2 x^{2} + y^{2}\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=4 x\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{u}\right)&=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u}}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u}}\right)\cdot\left(4 x\right)\\
&=\frac{2 x}{\sqrt{2 x^{2} + y^{2}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=1$ and $y=- \sqrt{2}$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=2 \left(1\right)^{2} + \left(- \sqrt{2}\right)^{2}=4.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(1,- \sqrt{2})&=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u_0}}\right)\cdot\left(4\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot\left(4\right)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=- 2 x^{2} y^{3} + e^{- 2 x y}$, evaluate $f_x(0,1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- 2 x y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=- 2 y\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(e^{u}\right)&=\left(e^{u}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(- 2 x^{2} y^{3}\right)&=- 4 x y^{3}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(e^{u}\right)\cdot\left(- 2 y\right)+\left(- 4 x y^{3}\right)\\
&=- 4 x y^{3} - 2 y e^{- 2 x y}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=0$ and $y=1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=- 2 \left(0\right) \left(1\right)=0.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(0,1)&=\left(e^{u_0}\right)\cdot\left(-2\right)+\left(0\right)\\
&=\left(1\right)\cdot\left(-2\right)+\left(0\right)\\
&=-2.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\left(1 - x\right)^{3 y + 1}$, evaluate $f_x(-1,1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=1 - x\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=-1\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}u^{3 y + 1}&=\left(3 y + 1\right)\,u^{3 y}\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(u^{3 y} \left(3 y + 1\right)\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)\\
&=- \left(1 - x\right)^{3 y} \left(3 y + 1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-1$ and $y=1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=1 - \left(-1\right)=2.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(-1,1)&=\left(u_0^{3 \left(1\right)} \left(3 \left(1\right) + 1\right)\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)\\
&=\left(32\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)\\
&=-32.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for $1 - x>0$.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} y^{2} - \cos{\left(x y \right)}$, evaluate $f_y(- \frac{\pi}{2},-1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $x$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=x y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=x\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(- \cos{\left(u \right)}\right)&=\left(\sin{\left(u \right)}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(2 x^{2} y^{2}\right)&=4 x^{2} y\\
f_y(x,y)&=\left(\sin{\left(u \right)}\right)\cdot\left(x\right)+\left(4 x^{2} y\right)\\
&=4 x^{2} y + x \sin{\left(x y \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=- \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $y=-1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=\left(- \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \left(-1\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(- \frac{\pi}{2},-1)&=\left(\sin{\left(u_0 \right)}\right)\cdot\left(- \frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\left(- \pi^{2}\right)\\
&=\left(1\right)\cdot\left(- \frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\left(- \pi^{2}\right)\\
&=- \pi \left(\frac{1}{2} + \pi\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\cos^{2}{\left(- x^{2} + 2 y \right)}$, evaluate $f_x(2,\frac{\pi}{4} + 2)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- x^{2} + 2 y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=- 2 x\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\cos^2(u)&=2\cos(u)\cdot(-\sin(u))\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(- 2 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cos{\left(u \right)}\right)\cdot\left(- 2 x\right)\\
&=4 x \sin{\left(- x^{2} + 2 y \right)} \cos{\left(- x^{2} + 2 y \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=2$ and $y=\frac{\pi}{4} + 2$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=- \left(2\right)^{2} + 2 \left(\frac{\pi}{4} + 2\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(2,\frac{\pi}{4} + 2)&=\left(- 2 \sin{\left(u_0 \right)} \cos{\left(u_0 \right)}\right)\cdot\left(-4\right)\\
&=\left(0\right)\cdot\left(-4\right)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{e^{- x y^{2}}}{x - y^{2} + 2},
$$

find $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$, where $x - y^{2} + 2\ne0$.
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=e^{- x y^{2}}$ and $D=x - y^{2} + 2$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=- 2 x y e^{- x y^{2}}, \\
D_{y}&=- 2 y.
\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule differentiates the exponent first; its inner derivative is $- 2 x y$. Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- 2 x y e^{- x y^{2}}\right)D-N\left(- 2 y\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{e^{- x y^{2}}\left(- 2 x^{2} y + 2 x y^{3} - 4 x y + 2 y\right)}{\left(x - y^{2} + 2\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step factors the common nonzero exponential $e^{- x y^{2}}$ from the numerator.  These expressions apply where $x - y^{2} + 2\ne0$.

:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{e^{x y^{2}}}{x + y^{2} - 2},
$$

find $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$, where $x + y^{2} - 2\ne0$.
:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}

The chain rule differentiates the exponent first; its inner derivative is $y^{2}$. Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

&=\frac{\left(y^{2} e^{x y^{2}}\right)D-N\left(1\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{e^{x y^{2}}\left(x y^{2} + y^{4} - 2 y^{2} - 1\right)}{\left(x + y^{2} - 2\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step factors the common nonzero exponential $e^{x y^{2}}$ from the numerator.  These expressions apply where $x + y^{2} - 2\ne0$.

f_y(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2 x^{2}\right)\\
&=2 x^{2} + \frac{e^{x^{2} + y}}{e^{x^{2} + y} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=1$ and $y=0$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=\left(1\right)^{2} + \left(0\right)=1.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(1,0)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{e}{1 + e}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2\right)\\
&=\frac{2 + 3 e}{1 + e}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

\end{aligned}

Substitute $x=1$ and $y=-1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=- \left(1\right) \left(-1\right)=1.

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(1,-1)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(1\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{e}{1 + e}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(1\right)\\
&=\frac{1 + 2 e}{1 + e}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Treat $x$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- x y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=- x\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\ln(1+e^u)&=\frac{1}{1+e^u}\cdot e^u\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(x y^{2}\right)&=2 x y\\
f_y(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(- x\right)+\left(2 x y\right)\\
&=2 x y - \frac{x e^{- x y}}{1 + e^{- x y}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=1$ and $y=-1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=- \left(1\right) \left(-1\right)=1.

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(1,-1)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)+\left(-2\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{e}{1 + e}\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)+\left(-2\right)\\
&=\frac{- 3 e - 2}{1 + e}.

$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ given that $f(x,y) = 3x\ln y + 2ye^x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+2{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{1}{y}+2{e}^{x}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3x}{y}+2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y) = y^2\ln{x},$ express $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ as the limit of a difference quotient.
:question/worked-solution:
The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit 

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}\right).
$$

Since $f(x) = y^2 \ln{x},$  we have that 

$$
f(x+h,y) = y^2\ln(x+h).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0}\left( \dfrac{y^2\ln(x+h) -y^2\ln{x} }{h}\right).
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y) = x^2y^2+\sin{x}\cos{y},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(\pi,2\pi).$

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot (2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,2\pi )} & =2\cdot \pi \cdot (2\pi )^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2\pi \cdot 4{\pi }^{2}+(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =8{\pi }^{3}-1\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x-8{y}^{2}.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x-8{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{y}^{2}) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x)-8{y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂x}(1) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}-0 \\  & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}

The notation ${f}_{y}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y.$

:question/problem:

:question/problem:
For the function $f(x,y)=x^2y+y^3$, evaluate $f_x(2,3)$.

Treat $y$ as a constant when differentiating with respect to $x$.

Hold $y$ fixed. The factor $y$ in $x^2y$ is constant, and the entire term $y^3$ is constant with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=y\frac{d}{dx}(x^2)+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(y^3)\\
&=y(2x)+0\\
&=2xy.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute the coordinates into the derivative:

$$
f_x(2,3)=2\cdot2\cdot3=12.
$$

The requested value is a derivative value, rather than the function value $f(2,3)=39$.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=y^2\sqrt{x}+\frac{x}{y}$, evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(9,3)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, holding $x$ fixed. In particular, $\sqrt{x}$ and $x$ are constant factors. Rewrite the reciprocal as a negative power:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(y^2\sqrt{x}+xy^{-1}\right)\\
&=\sqrt{x}(2y)+x(-y^{-2})\\
&=2y\sqrt{x}-\frac{x}{y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate both contributions at $(9,3)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(9,3)&=2\cdot3\cdot\sqrt{9}-\frac{9}{3^2}\\
&=18-1\\
&=17.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=x\sec y+x^4y$, evaluate $f_y\left(\sqrt{2},-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)&=x\frac{d}{dy}(\sec y)+x^4\frac{d}{dy}(y)\\
&=x\sec y\tan y+x^4.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the given point, the exact values are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sec\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\sqrt{2},\\
\tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=-1,\\
(\sqrt{2})^4&=4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these into the derivative and combine the two contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y\left(\sqrt{2},-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
&=\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}\cdot(-1)+4\\
&=-2+4\\
&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\ln(2xy)$ on the domain $xy>0,$ which limit of a difference quotient represents $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$?
:question/worked-solution:
For the partial derivative with respect to $y,$ hold $x$ constant and use

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x,y+h)-f(x,y)}{h}.
$$

Replace the whole input $y$ by $y+h$ inside the logarithm:

$$
f(x,y+h)=\ln\bigl(2x(y+h)\bigr).
$$

The factor $2x$ still multiplies the incremented input. Thus the logarithm's argument is $2xy+2xh,$ not $2xy+h.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\ln\bigl(2x(y+h)\bigr)-\ln(2xy)}{h}.
$$

Here $x$ is fixed and $h\ne 0$ before taking the limit. Since $xy>0,$ sufficiently small increments keep the logarithm defined.

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy+y^2}{x+2y}$ on the domain $x+2y\ne 0,$ which limit of a difference quotient represents $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$?
:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant. The definition requires

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x,y+h)-f(x,y)}{h}.
$$

Every occurrence of $y$ in the incremented function value must change: the $y$ in $xy,$ the input being squared, and the $y$ in the denominator. Hence

$$
f(x,y+h)=\frac{x(y+h)+(y+h)^2}{x+2(y+h)}.
$$

Subtract the entire original fraction and divide the difference by $h$:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\left(\frac{x(y+h)+(y+h)^2}{x+2(y+h)}-\frac{xy+y^2}{x+2y}\right).
$$

Changing only the numerator or only the denominator does not give $f(x,y+h).$ Changing $x$ as well would also violate the definition. Here $h\ne 0$ before taking the limit; $x+2y\ne 0$ ensures that sufficiently small increments keep both function values defined.

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2xy^2,$ which limit of a difference quotient represents $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$?
:question/worked-solution:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}.
$$

Substituting $x+h$ for $x$ gives

$$
f(x+h,y)=2(x+h)y^2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{2(x+h)y^2-2xy^2}{h}.
$$

Only the $x$ coordinate changes. The numerator subtracts the original function value from the incremented value, and $h\ne 0$ before taking the limit.

:question/problem: Find $f_x(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=e^{3x+2y}+x^2y^2.$
:question/worked-solution:
The notation $f_x$ means the partial derivative with respect to $x$. Hold $y$ constant, so $e^{2y}$ and $y^2$ are constant multipliers. First write $e^{3x+2y}=e^{2y}e^{3x}$.

Using the sum and constant multiple rules,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(e^{2y}e^{3x})+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2y^2) \\
&=e^{2y}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(e^{3x})+y^2\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2) \\
&=e^{2y}\cdot 3e^{3x}+y^2\cdot 2x \\
&=3e^{3x+2y}+2xy^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
The factor $3$ comes from differentiating $e^{3x}$; the held factor $e^{2y}$ is unchanged.

:question/problem: Find $f_y(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=x\ln y+y\ln x+e^{2x+y}+\dfrac{x}{y}$, where $x>0$ and $y>0$.
:question/worked-solution:
The notation $f_y$ means the partial derivative with respect to $y$. Treat $x$ as constant throughout. In particular, $\ln x$ is a constant multiplier in $y\ln x$, whereas $\ln y$ must be differentiated in $x\ln y$.

Rewrite $e^{2x+y}=e^{2x}e^y$ and $x/y=xy^{-1}$ to expose the constant multipliers. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)
&=x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\ln y)
  +\ln x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y) \\
&\quad +e^{2x}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(e^y)
  +x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^{-1}) \\
&=x\cdot\frac{1}{y}+\ln x\cdot 1+e^{2x}\cdot e^y+x\cdot(-y^{-2}) \\
&=\frac{x}{y}+\ln x+e^{2x+y}-\frac{x}{y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here $x$ survives as a multiplier in the first and last terms. The last term is negative because the derivative of $y^{-1}$ is $-y^{-2}$.

:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ given that $f(x,y)=x^2\cos y+y^3.$

$$

:question/problem: Find $f_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=x e^{y}+y e^{x}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(x e^{y}) &=x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{y}) \\
&=x\cdot \left(e^{y}\right) \\
&=x e^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y e^{x}) &=e^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\
&=e^{x}\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=x e^{y} + e^{x}$.

$$

Therefore $f_{x}(x,y)=y e^{x} + 2 e^{y}$.

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(e^{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(e^{2},1)} & =4 (1)^{3} \ln{(e^{2})}+\frac{(e^{2})}{2 \sqrt{(1)}} \\  & =\frac{e^{2}}{2} + 8\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The substitution $z=y^m$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}}
$$

into an equation of the form $z'(x) + P(x)z(x) = Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = x^3, \qquad q(x) = 1, \qquad n=-\dfrac12.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by $y^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
y^{1/2} \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y^{3/2}= 1.\qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = \dfrac{3}{2}y^{1/2} \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y^{1/2}\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(\ast)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + x^3\,z = 1
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{3}{2}x^3z = \dfrac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}.$

:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{y}{x}  = \dfrac{x^2}{y} .
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad q(x) = x^2, \qquad n=-1.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by $y^{-1},$ and we get

$$
y \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{x}= x^2.
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2y \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{1}{x}z  = x^2
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{2}{x} z
		=2x^2
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=2{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2{x}^{2}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =2{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2}) & =2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{x}^{2} & =\frac{2{x}^{5}}{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{2{x}^{5}+C}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5C_1.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z=y^{2}.$ This results in the general solution

$$
y^{ 2} =\dfrac{2x^5 + C}{5x^2}.
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following equations is a Bernoulli differential equation?

- $y\,y' + x^2y^2 = e^x y^4$

- $xy' + x^3y = -x^2 y^3$

- $y' + y\cos{x} = e^{y+1}$
:question/worked-solution:
A Bernoulli differential equation has the form

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n,
$$

where $n$ is a real number.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Equation I is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
y' + x^2y = e^x y^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) = e^x, \qquad n=3.
$$

- Equation II is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
y' + x^2y = -xy^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) =-x, \qquad n=3.
$$

- Equation III is *not* a Bernoulli differential equation. It is missing the $q(x)y^n$ term.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}y=x{y}^{4}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{2},\,q(x)=x,\,n=4.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{-3}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-3{y}^{-4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z=x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2}z=-3x.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-3{x}^{2}.$

:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=x\sqrt{y}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{{y}^{1/2}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\,z=x
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{2x}\,z=\frac{x}{2}.

Therefore, $Q(x)=\frac{x}{2}.$

:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-1,\,q(x)={e}^{x},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-1}={e}^{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z={e}^{x}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-{e}^{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=1,\,Q(x)=-{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-{e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{x} & =-{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x}) & =-{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =-\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{C-{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/worked-solution:

I has this form with $n=2$. II has a $y^2$ term instead of the required linear $P(x)y$ term. III has this form with $n=-1/2$, on its real domain $y>0$.

:question/problem:
Which of the following equations is a Bernoulli differential equation?

1. $yy^{′} + x^{2}y^{3} = e^{x}y^{4}$
2. $y^{2}y^{′} + x^{2}y^{3} = e^{x}y^{4}$
3. $y^{′} + x^{2}\sin y = x\cos^{3} y$
:question/worked-solution:
A Bernoulli equation has the form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)y^n$ with $n\ne0,1$.

For I, division by $y$ gives $y'+x^2y^2=e^xy^3$, which still has two nonlinear powers. For II, division by $y^2$ gives
$$
y'+x^2y=e^xy^2,
$$
which is Bernoulli with $n=2$ on intervals where $y\ne0$. The original II also admits $y=0$, which should be checked separately when solving. III contains trigonometric functions of $y$ and does not have Bernoulli form.

Therefore the correct selection is **II only**.

:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-y(2x+3{y}^{2})=0
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-y(2x+3{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy-3{y}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy & =3{y}^{3} \\ \frac{dy}{dx}-2{x}^{-1}y & =3{x}^{-2}{y}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-2{x}^{-1},\,q(x)=3{x}^{-2},\,n=3.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}-2{x}^{-1}{y}^{-2}=3{x}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2{x}^{-1}z=3{x}^{-2}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+4{x}^{-1}z=-6{x}^{-2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-6{x}^{-2}.$

:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transform the differential equation

$$
{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2}-y=0
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2}-y & =0 \\ {y}^{1/2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2} & =y \\ \frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}y & ={y}^{1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{2},\,q(x)=1,\,n=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{1/2}=1.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z=1
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,z=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.$
